infovae-divergence-sign.title: InfoVAE: Balancing Learning and Inference in Variational Autoencoders
infovae-divergence-sign.version: arXiv:1706.02262v3, 30 May 2018; published AAAI 2019 version also inspected
infovae-divergence-sign.summary: InfoVAE penalizes disagreement between the encoder’s latent distribution and the prior. Proposition 2 permits replacing the marginal KL term by any strict divergence, but its parameter range allows the coefficient of that penalty to become negative. The objective then rewards disagreement. For α=0, λ=1/2 and D=3 KL, shifting an independent Gaussian encoder to mean m leaves its mutual information at zero while increasing the objective by m²/4. The matched model at m=0 cannot be a global maximum.

checks.location: Proposition 2, PDF p.4; Appendix A proof, PDF pp.11-12; objective Eq.(6)
checks.claim: Proposition 2 states that, at a fixed encoder mutual information, replacing the marginal KL term by any strict divergence preserves global optimality of a model that matches the data and has exact amortized inference, assuming α<1 and λ>0.
checks.explanation: The allowed range includes $\alpha+\lambda-1<0$, so the objective rewards the substituted divergence. Multiplying KL by a positive constant still gives a strict divergence. That reward can therefore exceed the remaining KL penalty. The appendix treats these terms as nonnegative penalties without establishing the needed coefficient sign.
checks.demonstration: Let $p_D(x)=p_\theta(x\mid z)=\mathcal N(0,1)$ and $p(z)=\mathcal N(0,1)$. Choose the encoder $q_m(z\mid x)=\mathcal N(m,1)$ independently of $x$, keeping $I_{q_m}(X;Z)=0$ and reconstruction fixed. With $\alpha=0$, $\lambda=1/2$, and $D=3D_{\mathrm{KL}}$, all stated parameter conditions hold and $D$ is strict. Since $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathcal N(m,1)\|\mathcal N(0,1))=m^2/2$, $$\widehat{\mathcal L}(m)=-H(p_D)-\frac{m^2}{2}+\frac{3m^2}{4}=-H(p_D)+\frac{m^2}{4}.$$ The model at $m=0$ has the correct data marginal and exact posterior, but $m=2$ improves its objective by $1$. The objective is unbounded above along this family.
checks.repair: Add $\alpha+\lambda-1\ge0$ to the proposition. For finite entropy and KL terms, the chain rule gives $$\widehat{\mathcal L}=-H(p_D)+\alpha I_q(X;Z)-\mathbb E_{q(z)}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q(x\mid z)\|p_\theta(x\mid z))-(1-\alpha)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q(z)\|p(z))-(\alpha+\lambda-1)D(q(z)\|p(z)).$$ At fixed $I_q(X;Z)$, all three subtracted quantities are nonnegative under the corrected conditions. A representable matched joint with that mutual information sets them to zero and therefore attains the global upper bound. The boundary $\alpha+\lambda-1=0$ is also valid.
checks.scope: The issue concerns Proposition 2 after replacing aggregate KL by an arbitrary strict divergence. For $D=D_{\mathrm{KL}}$, the aggregate penalties combine to $-\lambda D_{\mathrm{KL}}$, so this witness does not apply. The sufficient repair narrows the parameter range and requires a representable matched joint at the prescribed mutual information.
checks.whyItMatters: The optimality guarantee for arbitrary strict divergences fails in part of the stated parameter range. Requiring $\alpha+\lambda-1\ge0$ restores the guarantee when the model family contains an exact matched joint with the prescribed mutual information.
checks.title: InfoVAE’s divergence substitution needs a coefficient restriction
checks.claimContext: Proposition 2 allows the aggregate KL divergence in the InfoVAE objective to be replaced by any strict divergence $D$. It claims that, for $\alpha<1$ and $\lambda>0$, an exact data model with exact inference is a global maximizer at each fixed encoder mutual information. Here $p_D$ is the data distribution, $q(z\mid x)$ the encoder, $p_\theta(x\mid z)$ the decoder, $p(z)$ the latent prior, and $q(z)$ the encoder’s aggregate latent distribution.
checks.claimFormula: \widehat{\mathcal L}=\mathbb E_{p_D(x)q(z\mid x)}\log p_\theta(x\mid z)-(1-\alpha)\mathbb E_{p_D(x)}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q(z\mid x)\|p(z))-(\alpha+\lambda-1)D(q(z)\|p(z)).
checks.checkedLocation: Proposition 2 and Eq. (6), PDF p.4; Appendix A proof, PDF pp.11–12

infovae-divergence-sign.paperSummary: A variational autoencoder learns an encoder from data to hidden variables and a decoder back to data. InfoVAE changes its training objective to balance generation, inference, and the information retained in those hidden variables. It introduces adjustable weights and alternative ways to compare the aggregate latent distribution with the model's prior.
infovae-divergence-sign.theoryRole: Proposition 2 supports the use of alternative divergence measures by asserting that exact data and inference matching remain globally optimal at a fixed mutual information. It provides an idealized optimization justification for the broader objective family.

review-neurips-2026-139193.title: Crossing the Validation crisis: Cross-validation reduces benchmarking variance surprisingly well

checks.claim: Ranking retrieval tends1 asN orK increases.
checks.explanation: Increasing $K$ averages over partitions of the same observations. It removes randomness from the choice of partition but retains the error caused by drawing a finite study set. Distinct population scores and paired comparisons do not remove that error. The paper already identifies the corresponding nonzero variance floor after Eq. (9).
checks.demonstration:
Let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_5$ be independent Bernoulli labels with success probability $3/5$. Compare two learning rules that always predict $1$ and $0$, regardless of their four training observations. Their population accuracies are $3/5$ and $2/5$, so the oracle order is strict and does not depend on training size. On each paired split, hold out one uniformly chosen observation. If $S=\sum_{i=1}^{5}Y_i$, the two mean accuracies converge almost surely to $S/5$ and $1-S/5$ as $K\to\infty$. Because $5$ is odd, these conditional limits cannot tie. The oracle order is therefore recovered exactly when $S\ge3$, giving
\[
\begin{aligned}
\lim_{K\to\infty}\pi_K(5)
&=\sum_{s=3}^{5}\binom{5}{s}(3/5)^s(2/5)^{5-s}\\
&=\frac{2133}{3125}=0.68256<1.
\end{aligned}
\]
 Both estimators are unbiased; their error comes entirely from variance. In fact, the variance of the first mean accuracy is $6/125+24/(125K)$, which decreases with $K$ and approaches a positive limit.
checks.repair:
At fixed $N$, let $D$ be the random study dataset and $Z_{k,m}$ the split-$k$ score of algorithm $F_m$. Suppose the split-score vectors are conditionally independent and identically distributed given $D$, with integrable components. Define $\mu_m(D)=\mathbb E[Z_{1,m}\mid D]$. The conditional strong law gives $K^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{K}Z_{k,m}\to\mu_m(D)$ almost surely. If the conditional means are pairwise distinct almost surely, the limiting ranking-retrieval probability is the probability that their order agrees with the population order. This equals one only when that conditional order is correct almost surely. Conditional ties need separate analysis; distinct population scores alone do not exclude them.

For a growing-data claim, let $K_N$ be the chosen number of splits, $R^*_{m,N}$ the population score of algorithm $m$ at the training size used by those splits, and $\delta_N>0$ the smallest adjacent gap in the oracle order. Use that same population score as the estimator's target. For fixed finite $M$, the condition $\max_m|\widehat R_{K_N}(F_m;N)-R^*_{m,N}|=o_p(\delta_N)$ is sufficient: when every error is below $\delta_N/2$, no pair reverses or ties. One sufficient mean-square condition is $\sum_{m=1}^{M}\mathbb E[(\widehat R_{K_N}(F_m;N)-R^*_{m,N})^2]=o(\delta_N^2)$. These conditions must be established for the learning procedure; they do not imply monotonicity at finite $N$ or $K$. The ranking-equivalent sample gain also requires a common oracle order across the study sizes being compared.
checks.scope: The counterexample concerns the universal convergence assertion after Eq. (H.1). It preserves strict population ordering, paired splits, the $80/20$ training/test fraction and unbiased scores. It does not contradict the reported empirical variance reductions or establish monotonicity for general learning rules.
checks.title: Repeated splits retain finite-sample ranking error
checks.whyItMatters: A fixed dataset can remain below a desired ranking-retrieval probability regardless of the number of splits. The threshold-crossing sample gain in Appendix H is meaningful at levels that are actually reachable; increasing $K$ alone does not guarantee their attainability.
checks.claimContext: Appendix H considers a finite family of $M$ learning algorithms with distinct population scores, a fixed oracle order and paired Monte Carlo cross-validation splits. Let $N$ be the study-set size, $K$ the number of splits, and $\pi_K(N)$ the probability, over the study sample and splits, that the estimated order matches the full oracle order. The paragraph after Eq. (H.1) says this probability approaches one when either $N$ or $K$ grows, in a regime where score variance dominates the comparison. The claim below takes $K\to\infty$ while holding $N$ fixed.
checks.checkedLocation: Appendix H, Eq. (H.1) and following paragraph, p.33; Eq. (9), pp.4–5

checks.explanation: No issue was found in the checked claims. The noisy-regression counterexample does not refute the ordering in the stated noiseless family. The source already distinguishes the two noise regimes.
checks.demonstration: For \(\beta\sim N(0,I)\), conditional on the design matrix with eigenvalues \(\lambda_j>0\), the integrated ridge excess prediction risk is \[R(\alpha)=\sum_j\frac{\alpha^2+\sigma^2\lambda_j}{(\lambda_j+\alpha)^2}.\] Its derivative is \[R\!\prime(\alpha)=2\sum_j\frac{\lambda_j(\alpha-\sigma^2)}{(\lambda_j+\alpha)^3}.\] With the stated noiseless choice \(\sigma=0\), this is nonnegative for \(\alpha\ge0\). With \(\sigma>0\), the derivative can be negative below \(\sigma^2\), but that establishes a limitation of extending the claim to a different noise regime, not an error in the noiseless ordering.

checks.claim: CLT supplies exact finite-sample Student distribution.
checks.explanation: The central limit theorem does not imply an exact finite-sample Student law. Exact Student calibration additionally requires independent identically distributed Gaussian differences under the null.
checks.demonstration: Under the null, let each difference independently equal \(-1\) or \(1\) with equal probability. The sample mean and variance, hence the studentized statistic when defined, have discrete distributions. With probability \(2^{1-S}\), all signs agree and the sample variance is zero. This cannot be the continuous \(t_{S-1}\) law. With independent identically distributed differences of mean zero and finite positive variance, the CLT and consistency of the sample variance instead give asymptotic standard normality.
checks.repair: Call the paired test an asymptotic approximation under independent identically distributed differences with finite positive variance. If exact \(t_{S-1}\) calibration is claimed, add the Gaussian-difference hypothesis; the usual independence of the normal sample mean and chi-square sample variance then proves it.
checks.scope: A local calibration statement needs correction. This does not establish that any reported significance decision changes.
checks.title: The CLT gives approximate, not exact, Student calibration
checks.claimContext: Appendix G.2 forms a paired statistic from \(S\) independent experimental differences and attributes a finite-sample \(t_{S-1}\) distribution to the central limit theorem, without assuming Gaussian differences.

checks.demonstration: Discarding one singular direction of matrix \(i\) saves \(m_i+n_i\) parameters. These savings differ across matrix shapes, whereas ordering singular values alone ranks error increments without accounting for their different savings. For normalized spectra with nonzero squared singular values \((0.96,0.04)\) in an \(8\times8\) matrix and \((0.455,0.455,0.09)\) in a \(16\times16\) matrix, retaining their nonzero ranks costs 128 parameters. To meet a 96-parameter budget, discarding only the second matrix’s smallest direction costs error 0.09 and reaches 96. Pooled greedy truncation discards the 0.04 direction first, remains at 112, then discards the 0.09 direction and reaches 80 with error 0.13. Both outcomes satisfy the stated compression guards from 0.05 to 0.8. This shows why the former global-optimality inference was too strong. It is compatible with the revised procedure’s explicitly heuristic status.
checks.scope: Current v2 resolves the retained optimality overstatement. The allocation algorithm can be useful without attaining a globally minimal reconstruction error at a heterogeneous storage budget.
